name: Rosa Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and won't be traced back to you. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Totally fine. I talk about this stuff all the time anyway, usually to people who wish I'd stop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead designer at a five-person studio that does adverts and social campaigns for local shops, a small gym chain and the council's recycling posters. I start every morning by running the day's briefs through two or three AI tools to get rough directions, then I spend the rest of the day making them actually good. I love the speed now, honestly; I can show a client six ideas before lunch. What wears me out is the money: I rent a tiny flat above a bakery, I earn less than the city studios pay, and I've got about ten days of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I'd bet on the tools getting much better. I'd post something like: fine, back to doing it properly, it was fun while it lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep a small edge, because I'm faster than most designers round here with the tools as they are. But my pay doesn't move, and the studio still lives month to month on shop owners who pay in sixty days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools for first drafts and teach the other two designers my shortcuts, which I've been meaning to do. I'd ask the boss to put my speed into my pay, maybe a ten percent rise. And I'd finally open a separate savings account and auto-move eighty a month into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, a bit relieved. The ceiling's lower than I hoped, but the floor's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the studio lives month to month. How close to the edge is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Close. Last spring the gym chain paused its campaign for two months and the boss cut everyone to four days. A four-day week on my wage means I'm choosing between the phone bill and the bus pass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a small time saving change how many people the studio needs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one fewer hire next year, not a firing. Our junior designer might not get replaced if he leaves. That's the quiet way small studios shrink.

say: I'd say I'm **a bit disappointed**, because I'd bet on the tools improving.
I'd post that it's **back to doing it properly**.
think: I keep a **small edge**, being faster with the tools than most local designers.
My pay stays put while the studio waits **sixty days** for shops to pay.
do: Teach the other designers her **AI shortcuts** for first drafts.
Ask for a **ten percent rise** based on her speed.
Move **eighty a month** automatically into a new savings account.
feel: **Flat and relieved**: a lower ceiling, but the floor's still there.
S0.quote: A four-day week on my wage means I'm choosing between the phone bill and the bus pass.
fieldNote: She's the **rare enthusiast**, mildly disappointed that the tools stall.
Her real fear is **lost hours**, which already happened once when a client paused.
She notices the **quiet shrinking** of small studios through unreplaced jobs.

steps.text: Teach the two other designers her AI first-draft shortcuts
Ask the boss for a ten percent rise based on speed
Set up an automatic eighty-a-month transfer to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: the tools are good, the bosses who use them to cut jobs are the problem. I'd push for designers to get a share of what these companies make, and for small studios to get support to adapt rather than fold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm one of the safer people in the studio, which feels grim to say. I already work this way. But the studio might go from five to three, and the shops might start making their own ads, so even the survivors get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a weekend workshop for local shop owners on using AI for their own posters, charging twenty-five a head, because they're going to do it anyway and I'd rather they did it well. I'd build a portfolio of AI-assisted campaigns to show I can direct the tools, not just press buttons. And I'd get the other two designers into the freelancers' union with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Excited and worried at once, like the night before a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be teaching shop owners to do the work your studio sells. Isn't that cutting your own branch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, a bit. But the shop owners will do it anyway, badly, and they'll pay someone who shows them how. I'd rather teach the bakery downstairs to make its own posters than watch it hire an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the colleagues who don't use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with them on a real job, not lecture them. Our older designer Pat hates it all, and I get why. But I'd rather drag Pat along than watch the boss replace a person with a subscription.

say: I'd say the **tools are good**; bosses cutting jobs with them are the problem.
I'd push for **small studios** to get support to adapt rather than fold.
think: I'm one of the **safer people** in the studio, which feels grim to admit.
The studio could **shrink from five to three** as shops make their own ads.
do: Run **weekend workshops** for shop owners at twenty-five a head.
Bring her colleagues into the **freelancers' union**.
feel: **Wired**, excited and worried at once, like before a new job.
S1.quote: I'd rather teach the bakery downstairs to make its own posters than watch it hire an app.
fieldNote: She knowingly **undercuts her studio** by teaching clients, and accepts the contradiction.
She expects the **studio to shrink**, which threatens even her hours.
Her progressive view targets **bosses**, not the tools themselves.

steps.text: Run weekend AI poster workshops for shop owners at twenty-five a head
Build a portfolio of AI-directed ad campaigns
Sign up herself and two colleagues to the freelancers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to steer, so governments need to slow the rollout and fund people through it. I'd be posting about a basic income every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good at the tools doesn't save me when the tools don't need me. All of my work is thinking work, so 2028 is the end for my design job. My edge lasts maybe six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend those two years cramming money in: every freelance job I can get, evenings and weekends, so I have a few months' cushion. I'd look at moving back in with my mum and stepdad to stop paying rent. And I'd learn something hands-on, maybe exhibition building or set building, which gets the three robot years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I've been running fast in the right direction and someone's just moved the finish line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your mum and stepdad react?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would say yes and then ask every day about my plans. My stepdad has run a scaffolding firm for twenty years, and he'd tease me about my master's degree. He'd also probably give me a job, which is the bit I'd hate admitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still teach those workshops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year, maybe, while people still need someone to hold their hand. After that, the AI teaches itself. My workshop idea has a two-year shelf life in this picture.

say: I'd say governments should **slow the rollout** and fund people through it.
I'd post about a **basic income** every day.
think: Being good with the tools **doesn't save me** when the tools don't need me.
My **edge lasts** maybe six months after 2028.
do: Take **every freelance job** for two years to build a few months' cushion.
Move back in with her **mum and stepdad** to stop paying rent.
Learn **set or exhibition building**, which gets the robot gap.
feel: **Alarmed**, as if the finish line moved while she was running.
S2.quote: Being good at the tools doesn't save me when the tools don't need me.
fieldNote: Even the **most adaptive** designer sees her edge vanish in two years.
Her backup is **family**: moving home and a possible scaffolding job.
She uses the **three-year robot gap** by looking at set building.

steps.text: Take every evening and weekend freelance job to build a cushion
Move back into her mum and stepdad's house
Learn set and exhibition building through a short course
Campaign online for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build a fair transition if we start right now. I'd be at the union meetings arguing for retraining money tied to every company that buys AI to cut staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can ride the tools for a while and then step off. I'd be thirty-two, which is young. The design work goes in 2031, but I'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move from making things to running projects: managing campaigns where AI does the drafts and I handle clients, budgets and printing. I'd save hard for two years, aiming at three months. And I'd do a part-time course in project management at the college, which the union partly pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but a bit thrilled. Five years feels like a puzzle I can solve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't running projects also thinking work that AGI could take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know that. But the people part, standing in a shop and calming down an owner who hates the colours, lasts a bit longer. I'm buying time, not a forever job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running something with other people, maybe a small co-op of designers and makers. I'd like to own a piece of the tools instead of renting them. If it all goes, I'd want to have built something that belongs to us.

say: I'd say five years is enough for a **fair transition** if we start now.
I'd argue at union meetings for **retraining money** tied to AI-buying firms.
think: I can **ride the tools** for a while and then step off.
**Design work** goes in 2031, but at thirty-two I'd still have options.
do: Move into **running campaigns** where AI drafts and she handles clients.
Save hard towards **three months** of costs.
Take a **project management course** part-paid by the union.
feel: **Anxious but a bit thrilled**, like solving a puzzle.
S3.quote: I'm buying time, not a forever job.
fieldNote: She is **clear-eyed** that project work is also exposed, and calls it buying time.
Her goal is **shared ownership** of tools through a co-op.
Five years shifts her from alarm to **active planning**.

steps.text: Take on campaign management where AI drafts and she handles clients
Save hard towards three months of living costs
Do a part-time project management course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do it right: retraining, ownership, a safety net. I'd want design schools teaching AI direction now, not pretending it isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is basically my whole thirties. I'd get to enjoy the good years with the tools and still have time to move on before 2036. I don't think graphic design as I know it survives, but I'll have done a lot by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and push the studio to sell AI-assisted campaign packages, which could actually grow us for a few years. I'd start the co-op idea slowly, with two other designers and a printer. And I'd save, because ten years of thin savings is how you end up stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the knot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll get comfortable. Ten years is long enough to forget the deadline. I've watched people at the studio ignore much smaller changes until the day they got the email.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change anything outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait to have kids until I see where the co-op lands. I'm not planning a family before thirty-two anyway. But I'd want them to grow up somewhere people still make things.

say: I'd say a decade is time for **retraining, ownership** and a safety net.
I'd want design schools teaching **AI direction** now.
think: I'd enjoy **the good years** with the tools and still move on before 2036.
**Graphic design** as I know it won't survive the decade.
do: Push the studio to sell **AI-assisted campaign** packages.
Start a **co-op** slowly with two designers and a printer.
Build real **savings** so thin money doesn't trap her.
feel: **Mostly hopeful**, with a knot about getting too comfortable.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to forget the deadline.
fieldNote: Her **biggest fear** is complacency, not the technology.
She still expects her **design income** to go, but sees a decade of opportunity first.
**Family plans** wait on whether the co-op takes hold.

steps.text: Pitch the studio an AI-assisted campaign package for local shops
Start a co-op with two designers and a local printer
Build savings steadily towards three months

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm the person who loves these tools, and even I lose in two years. What would help is a basic income or proper paid retraining, so people like me with ten days of savings aren't making life choices in a panic.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked whether people like me feel guilty. I sometimes do. Every shortcut I teach a shop owner is a job I helped shrink.

headlineQuote: Every shortcut I teach a shop owner is a job I helped shrink.
portrait: Rosa is a **lead designer** at a five-person ad studio and uses AI tools every day.
She rents a flat above a bakery, earns below city rates and has **ten days** of savings.
In slower pictures she sees opportunity: **workshops, campaign management** and a designers' co-op.
In **AGI by 2028**, she admits her edge vanishes and she'd move home to her mum and stepdad.
She carries some **guilt** about teaching clients to replace the work she sells.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: even as the most AI-ready designer, she loses her work in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** or paid retraining so thin-savings workers aren't choosing in panic.
